analysis.one_liner: Bans publicly traded corporations from spending money on federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: Senator Hawley introduced it alone with zero cosponsors, it sat in the Senate Rules Committee, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for publicly traded corporations and their affiliates to put money into federal elections — including direct contributions, donations to political committees, and spending on election ads. It would also be illegal for anyone to solicit or accept that money. The aim is to take corporate treasury money out of campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters and candidates who rely on individual donors rather than corporate money, since corporate treasuries could no longer fund campaigns or election ads. Shareholders also gain in a small way, because executives could no longer spend company money on politics.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a publicly traded corporation, or any company it controls, to contribute money to federal campaigns or to fund electioneering ads and independent expenditures.
Also makes it unlawful for anyone to solicit, accept, or receive corporate contributions, closing the pass-through route by which corporate money could reach campaigns.
If enforced, it would force federal campaigns to run on money from individuals rather than corporate treasuries, reducing the weight of large public-company money in elections.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded corporations and their affiliates, which would lose a legal channel for influencing federal elections, along with the super PACs and political committees that currently take their money. Candidates who depend on that money would have to replace it.
analysis.who_pays_short: Publicly traded corporations and corporate-funded political committees

drawbacks.text: The ban covers only publicly traded corporations and their affiliates. Privately held companies, wealthy individuals, and other big-money channels are untouched, so large sums could still flow into elections through other doors.

The Supreme Court held in Citizens United that corporate independent spending on elections is protected speech, so the parts of this bill barring independent expenditures and electioneering ads would very likely face a constitutional challenge even if passed.

The bill contains no provisions for public financing or other ways for candidates without wealthy backers to compete, so its practical effect would be to remove one money source without building another.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On paper this is a genuine reform: it would shut off a large and little-trusted source of campaign money. But it is a narrow version — it leaves private companies, unions, and individual megadonors untouched — and its ban on independent electioneering spending runs headlong into existing Supreme Court doctrine, so even a full passage might have been struck down or narrowed in court. The larger fact is that it never got that far: it was never debated, amended, or voted on at all.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Josh Hawley introduced the bill on October 31, 2023, near the end of the first session of the 118th Congress.
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor, from either party.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration, which was its only action; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, as any bill not passed by both chambers does.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Publicly traded corporations keep their existing ability to fund campaigns and election ads, and the political committees that accept their money keep that funding stream. No reform of corporate election money happened.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Publicly traded corporations and their political committees

for.name: Sen. Josh Hawley
for.what_they_did: Sole sponsor: introduced the bill and referred it to committee; no senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration (chaired by Sen. Amy Klobuchar)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, leaving it to die in committee.

against.name: The other 99 senators
against.what_they_did: Not one senator from either party cosponsored the bill during its 14 months of existence.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership under Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Long the leading opponent of campaign-finance restrictions in the Senate, arguing such limits unconstitutionally restrict political speech; the bill got no Republican support or floor action.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll call to measure; all that is known is that a Republican sponsored it alone and not a single senator of either party cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would end their ability to spend corporate treasury money on federal campaigns, election ads, and political committees — a channel their interest runs to keep open. Their stake is the direct target of the bill.

industries.industry: Corporate-funded super PACs and political committees
industries.note: Committees that rely on public-company money would lose that funding stream, since both giving and receiving corporate contributions would become unlawful.
